lessons.title: GCD and async/await Fundamentals

quickCheck.prompt: Why does calling `DispatchQueue.main.sync { }` from code already running on the main thread deadlock?
quickCheck.explanation: `DispatchQueue.main` is a serial queue: it runs one block at a time. `.sync` blocks the caller until the block finishes, but the block can never start because the queue is already occupied by the very code that's waiting on it.

options.text: The main queue is serial, so the queued block can't run while the caller is blocked waiting on it
DispatchQueue.main only accepts async submissions, so a sync call has no effect and never runs the block
The main thread has no dispatch queue attached until a run loop starts
Sync calls automatically retry on a background thread once the queue is busy

lessons.title: Actors & Data Isolation

quickCheck.prompt: How does an actor prevent a data race on its stored properties?
quickCheck.explanation: Actors serialize access to their isolated state — the runtime lets only one caller execute against it at a time, so concurrent unsynchronized writes simply can't happen.

options.text: By running every actor's code on one dedicated background thread for the whole app
By serializing access to its isolated state — only one caller executes at a time
By requiring every stored property to be declared with let
By wrapping every property access in an NSLock behind the scenes

lessons.title: Tasks & Structured Concurrency
lessons.body:
Swift offers several ways to start concurrent work, each with different inheritance and lifetime rules.

### `Task { }` vs `Task.detached { }`

`Task { }` created inside an actor-isolated or async context inherits that context's actor, priority, and task-local values. `Task.detached { }` starts a fresh, top-level task: no inherited actor, no inherited priority, no inherited task locals. Detached tasks are also **not** structured children — the enclosing scope doesn't wait for them, and cancelling the enclosing task doesn't cancel them.

### `async let` — implicit structured children

`async let` starts a child task immediately; the `await` is deferred until the value is actually needed. Multiple `async let` bindings run concurrently, and — being structured — each is automatically awaited or cancelled when its enclosing scope exits, even if you never explicitly await it yourself.

```swift
async let profile = fetchProfile(id: userID)
async let feed = fetchFeed(id: userID)
let (p, f) = try await (profile, feed)
```

### `TaskGroup` — dynamic fan-out

When the number of concurrent child tasks isn't known until runtime, `withTaskGroup(of:)` lets you `addTask` in a loop and collect results as they finish, not necessarily in submission order. Cancelling the group cancels every child that hasn't finished yet.

### Bridging callback APIs

`withCheckedContinuation` (and its throwing counterpart) wraps a legacy completion-handler API inside an `async` function. The continuation's `resume` must be called **exactly once** — calling it twice is a runtime misuse, and never calling it hangs the awaiting task forever.

### Cancellation

Cancellation is cooperative: marking a task cancelled just flips a flag. Long-running work should check `Task.isCancelled` (or call `try Task.checkCancellation()`) at sensible points and exit early.

quickCheck.prompt: In structured concurrency, when is a child task guaranteed to have finished?
quickCheck.explanation: Structured concurrency ties a child task's lifetime to its enclosing scope: the scope cannot return until every child task it created has completed or been cancelled and awaited.

options.text: Before the enclosing scope that created it returns
At some indeterminate point after the app is backgrounded
Only once the main actor becomes idle
Whenever the system scheduler next has a free core

lessons.title: Sendable, Races, Deadlocks & Swift 6 Checking
lessons.body:
Two failure modes get lumped together as 'concurrency bugs' but they're distinct. A **data race** is two threads touching the same mutable memory at once, with at least one write, and no synchronization — the outcome is undefined and often nondeterministic. A **deadlock** is threads or tasks each waiting on something the other holds, so neither ever proceeds — the outcome is a hang, not corruption.

### `Sendable`

A `Sendable` type is safe to move across concurrency domains — actor boundaries, `Task` closures — without introducing a data race. Value types made entirely of `Sendable` members are implicitly `Sendable`. Classes are not, by default, because references can be mutated from multiple places at once; a class can conform by being immutable, by synchronizing its own state internally, or — as an escape hatch you must justify — by being marked `@unchecked Sendable`.

### `@Sendable` closures and `nonisolated`

A closure typed `@Sendable` (required, for example, by `Task { }`'s initializer) must not capture non-Sendable mutable state by reference. `nonisolated` marks a member of an actor as exempt from actor isolation — callable without `await` — but it therefore cannot touch the actor's isolated mutable storage.

### Locks and semaphores vs actors

`DispatchSemaphore` and `NSLock` can serialize access the same way an actor does, but they block the calling thread while waiting, they aren't checked by the compiler, and misuse — such as waiting on a semaphore from the same serial queue that signals it — is a common deadlock source. An actor's `await` never blocks a thread; the thread is released back to the pool, and the compiler rejects unsynchronized access to isolated state at compile time.

### Swift 6 strict concurrency

Under the Swift 6 language mode, sendable-checking violations that used to be warnings become **compile errors**: passing non-`Sendable` state across an actor boundary, or capturing mutable state in a `@Sendable` closure, simply won't build.

quickCheck.prompt: Which best distinguishes a data race from a deadlock?
quickCheck.explanation: A data race is unsynchronized concurrent access to shared mutable state, with at least one write, producing undefined results. A deadlock is mutual waiting that never resolves, producing a hang rather than corrupted data.

options.text: A data race crashes the process outright; a deadlock merely slows it down
A deadlock corrupts memory; a data race merely wastes CPU cycles
A data race is unsynchronized concurrent access to shared state; a deadlock is mutual waiting that never completes
They're two names the compiler uses for the same diagnostic

questions.prompt: What distinguishes `DispatchQueue.main` from a queue returned by `DispatchQueue.global(qos:)`?
questions.explanation: `DispatchQueue.main` is a serial queue bound to the main thread — one block runs at a time, in order. Global queues are concurrent: the system can run multiple submitted blocks in parallel across worker threads.

options.text: DispatchQueue.main runs blocks in parallel across CPU cores; global queues run one at a time
Global queues can only be used for networking; DispatchQueue.main can run any kind of code
DispatchQueue.main is serial and thread-bound; global queues are concurrent
There is no practical difference — both ultimately run on the same worker threads

questions.prompt: An actor method does `let balance = accountBalance; await externalCall(); accountBalance = balance - amount`. Why is this risky?
questions.explanation: Actors are reentrant: at the `await`, another call is free to run on the actor and change `accountBalance` before the suspended method resumes. That method then overwrites the change using its stale, pre-await snapshot.

options.text: await blocks every other call to this actor for the rest of the app's lifetime, so it deadlocks waiting on itself
Another call can interleave during the await and mutate accountBalance before this method resumes
accountBalance is a global variable and isn't actor-isolated at all
Swift disallows reading a property before an await, so this line fails to compile

questions.prompt: You call `Task.detached { await self.sync() }` from inside a `@MainActor` method. What do you give up compared to plain `Task { }`?
questions.explanation: `Task { }` inherits the creating context's actor, priority, and task-local values. `Task.detached` starts an independent top-level task with none of that inherited — including no automatic @MainActor isolation.

options.text: Nothing — detached tasks behave identically to Task {} once they start running
Inheritance of the creating context's actor, priority, and task-local values
The ability to call async functions from inside the closure at all
Structured cancellation of any further child tasks the detached task itself spawns

questions.prompt: You write `async let a = fetchA(); async let b = fetchB()` followed later by `let (x, y) = try await (a, b)`. When do fetchA and fetchB actually start running?
questions.explanation: `async let` starts its child task immediately at the declaration, not at the await. Both run concurrently from the moment they're declared; the later await only collects results that may already be in progress.

options.text: Both start immediately at their async let declarations, running concurrently
Both start only once the await line is reached and executes
fetchA starts immediately; fetchB waits until fetchA finishes
The compiler reorders the two declarations based on which function has fewer parameters

questions.prompt: Why does updating a UIKit view from a background thread cause problems?
questions.explanation: UIKit's view hierarchy is not thread-safe; touching it off the main thread produces undefined behavior, including crashes and visual glitches. @MainActor confines UI code to the main thread and lets the compiler enforce it.

options.text: UIKit assumes single-threaded access to its view hierarchy
Background threads run at a reduced clock speed on iOS devices
UIView conforms to Sendable, which blocks writes from off the main thread
The main thread has exclusive access to the device's network stack

questions.prompt: What does checking `Task.isCancelled` inside a long-running task actually accomplish?
questions.explanation: Cancellation in Swift concurrency is cooperative — nothing stops a task automatically. Checking the flag lets your code notice a cancellation request and choose to stop early; ignoring it means the task keeps running to completion.

options.text: It immediately halts execution of the task at that exact line
It reports whether a cancellation request was sent, so the code can choose to stop early
It cancels every other task sharing the same executor
It throws a CancellationError automatically the very instant the flag would evaluate to true

questions.prompt: What does `await MainActor.run { updateLabel() }` do when called from a background task?
questions.explanation: MainActor.run hops the given closure onto the main actor and awaits its completion — a one-off way to run a piece of work on the main thread from any isolation context.

options.text: Blocks the background thread synchronously without ever yielding control back to the scheduler
Suspends the caller, runs the closure on the main actor, and resumes with its result
Schedules updateLabel to run after the current run loop cycle only
Only works if the enclosing type is already declared @MainActor

questions.prompt: What's wrong with this snippet under Swift's concurrency model?
questions.explanation: counter is mutable state captured and written from two independently scheduled tasks with no synchronization — a data race. The final printed value is not guaranteed, and Swift 6's strict checking flags this at compile time.

options.text: counter is mutable shared state written from two unsynchronized tasks — a data race
counter must be explicitly declared as var counter: Int = 0 or the file fails to compile
The two Task blocks run one after another, so print consistently shows 2
print(counter) captures a stale copy from before either task started

questions.prompt: What problem does marking a type Sendable actually solve?
questions.explanation: Sendable is a compile-time guarantee that a type's values can be passed across actor or task boundaries without introducing a data race — it's about concurrency safety, not serialization or networking.

options.text: It lets values of the type be encoded and sent over a network connection
It certifies the type is safe to share across concurrency domains without a data race
It makes every property of the type implicitly confined to one actor
It's a required prerequisite the compiler enforces before any type can conform to Codable

questions.prompt: A senior engineer says structured concurrency is more than sugar over `DispatchQueue.async`. What backs that claim?
questions.explanation: Structured concurrency ties child task lifetimes to their enclosing scope, propagates cancellation down the task tree automatically, and lets the type system express throwing/async contracts — none of which DispatchQueue's fire-and-forget closures provide on their own.

options.text: DispatchQueue.async blocks the submitting thread for the whole duration of the closure, while structured concurrency's tasks never do
Child task lifetimes are scoped, cancellation propagates automatically, and the type system enforces async/throws contracts
DispatchQueue queues cannot execute more than one closure, ever
Structured concurrency requires manually tracking a DispatchGroup for every child task

questions.prompt: You submit a block with `queue.sync { doWork() }`. What happens to the thread that made the call?
questions.explanation: `.sync` doesn't return control to the caller until the submitted block has finished executing — the calling thread is blocked for that entire duration, unlike `.async`, which returns immediately.

options.text: It's released back to the thread pool immediately, and doWork runs later
It runs doWork on a freshly spawned thread while the caller continues in parallel
It blocks until doWork finishes executing, then continues
It's suspended without consuming resources, exactly like an await

questions.prompt: This function is called while already executing on the main thread. What happens when it runs?
questions.explanation: DispatchQueue.main is serial. Calling .sync on it from code that's already running on the main thread asks the main queue to run a block and blocks waiting for it — but the queue can't start that block until the current, blocked work finishes. Neither side can proceed: a deadlock.

options.text: label.text updates normally, since calling sync from the main queue is just a stylistic choice here
The block runs on a background thread instead, to avoid blocking the caller
It throws a runtime error that Xcode reports as a data race
It deadlocks — the main queue can't run the block until the caller finishes waiting on it

questions.prompt: You submit three blocks, A then B then C, to the same serial `DispatchQueue`. What can you rely on?
questions.explanation: A serial queue runs one block at a time and starts each one only after the previous one finishes, in the order submitted — that ordering guarantee is exactly what 'serial' means.

options.text: A finishes before B starts, and B finishes before C starts
All three may run concurrently if the system has idle cores available
The queue picks whichever of the three blocks is fastest to run first
Order is only guaranteed if every block is marked @Sendable

questions.prompt: `queue` is a serial DispatchQueue. Why does this pattern hang?
questions.explanation: Both wait() and the async block are competing for the same serial queue's one execution slot. Because wait() runs on that same serial queue rather than a different thread, the signaling block can never get a turn to run — each side is waiting on the other.

options.text: DispatchSemaphore only works with concurrent queues, never serial ones
doSetup() throws an error partway through, so semaphore.signal() is never reached at all in this closure
wait() occupies the serial queue's only execution slot, so the block that would call signal() never runs
semaphore.wait() has a built-in timeout after a fixed system interval

questions.prompt: How do a data race and a deadlock differ in terms of observable failure?
questions.explanation: A data race is unsynchronized concurrent access to shared mutable state with at least one write — it produces nondeterministic, sometimes silently wrong, results. A deadlock is mutual waiting that never resolves — it produces a hang, with no corrupted data at all.

options.text: A data race terminates the running process immediately, while a deadlock only ever pauses execution for a moment
A deadlock corrupts shared memory; a data race merely wastes CPU time
They describe the same failure at different layers of the stack
A data race yields nondeterministic or corrupted results; a deadlock yields a permanent hang with no corruption

questions.prompt: Two callers invoke `withdraw(80)` on the same Account instance at nearly the same moment. Why might the balance go negative despite the guard check?
questions.explanation: The await inside logAttempt() is a suspension point. Both calls can pass the guard — balance is 100, and 80 <= 100 — before either has subtracted anything, because the actor is reentrant and lets the second call run during the first call's suspension. Each call then subtracts independently, taking balance below zero.

options.text: guard statements are evaluated lazily and never actually block execution
Actors run their methods on multiple threads simultaneously by default
Both calls can pass the guard before either await resumes, since the actor is reentrant
balance is declared with var, which fully disables the actor's isolation for that property

questions.prompt: You need to fetch an unknown number of thumbnails, decided at runtime, all concurrently, then collect every result. Which tool fits best?
questions.explanation: withTaskGroup lets you addTask in a loop for however many child tasks you need at runtime, then iterate over the group to collect results as they complete — exactly the dynamic-count case async let, fixed at compile time, doesn't cover.

options.text: async let, declared once per possible thumbnail ahead of time
Task.detached, called once per thumbnail with no group involved
withTaskGroup, adding one child task per thumbnail in a loop
DispatchQueue.concurrentPerform called from inside an async function

questions.prompt: If one of the addTask closures throws, what happens to the other in-flight child tasks in this group?
questions.explanation: When a child task in a throwing task group throws, the group rethrows on the next `for try await`, and — because task groups are structured — every remaining child task is automatically cancelled as the group's scope exits; none are left running.

options.text: The group cancels every remaining child task as it unwinds and rethrows the error
The other child tasks keep running to completion in the background, detached from the group
The whole process terminates immediately, since throwing task groups can't recover
fetchAll swallows the error and returns an empty array instead of throwing

questions.prompt: You need to call a legacy API that only offers `func load(completion: @escaping (Result<Data, Error>) -> Void)` from inside an `async` function. What's the idiomatic bridge?
questions.explanation: withCheckedThrowingContinuation hands you a continuation object; you call the legacy completion-based API inside the closure and resume the continuation exactly once with the result, turning the callback API into a normal awaitable call.

options.text: Wrap the call in Task.detached and poll a shared variable until it's set
Call it directly — Swift treats any completion handler as implicitly async
Use a DispatchSemaphore inside the async function to block until the completion handler eventually fires
Wrap it with withCheckedThrowingContinuation and resume exactly once inside the completion handler

questions.prompt: This code calls two legacy APIs, each of which can resume the same continuation. What's the concrete risk?
questions.explanation: withCheckedContinuation enforces resume-exactly-once; if both legacyLoad and legacyLoadFallback complete, resume is called a second time on an already-resumed continuation, which is a misuse the runtime flags rather than something that silently succeeds twice.

options.text: Nothing at all — the continuation simply returns whichever result arrives first and quietly ignores the rest
If both callbacks fire, resume gets called twice on the same continuation, which the runtime flags as misuse
The function never returns, because two callbacks conflict at compile time
legacyLoadFallback is automatically cancelled once legacyLoad starts running

questions.prompt: Inside a `@MainActor` method you write `Task.detached { self.updateModel() }` instead of `Task { self.updateModel() }`. What changes?
questions.explanation: Task.detached doesn't inherit the creating context's actor. updateModel() no longer runs with implicit @MainActor isolation just because the enclosing method was @MainActor — if updateModel touches main-actor state, it now needs its own isolation or an explicit hop.

options.text: Nothing — detached tasks still run on whatever actor created them
updateModel runs twice as fast because it skips actor isolation checks
updateModel loses the implicit @MainActor isolation inherited from the enclosing method
The compiler rejects this line outright, since detached tasks can't call instance methods at all

questions.prompt: What does marking a member of an actor `nonisolated` allow?
questions.explanation: nonisolated exempts a member from the actor's isolation, so it can be called synchronously without await from outside — but in exchange it can't read or write the actor's isolated mutable storage.

options.text: It can be called without await, but it can't touch the actor's isolated mutable state
It moves that member's execution onto a background thread pool instead of the actor's own executor
It gives every caller unrestricted, synchronized access to the actor's storage
It turns the member into a global actor reachable from anywhere in the app

questions.prompt: Your project builds cleanly under the Swift 5 language mode with minimal concurrency checking. What's the practical effect of switching the module to the Swift 6 language mode?
questions.explanation: Swift 6 makes complete data-race safety a build requirement rather than a warning: passing non-Sendable values across isolation boundaries, or capturing mutable state in a @Sendable closure, becomes a compile error instead of something that used to pass silently.

options.text: Nothing changes unless the deployment target is also raised
All DispatchQueue-based code is rejected in favor of async/await only
Actors are replaced at compile time with equivalent hand-written class-and-lock synchronization code
Sendable and isolation violations that used to be warnings, or invisible, become compile errors

questions.prompt: Under the Swift 6 language mode, what's flagged about capturing `counter` inside the `Task { }` closure?
questions.explanation: Task's closure is @Sendable, so anything it captures must be Sendable. Counter is a plain mutable class with no synchronization and no Sendable conformance, so capturing it here is exactly the kind of unsynchronized shared-state access strict checking is designed to catch.

options.text: Nothing — Task closures don't require anything they capture to be Sendable
value must be declared with let for the closure to compile at all
Counter is a non-Sendable mutable class captured by a @Sendable closure, flagged as unsafe
Task { } makes a fresh, independent copy of counter's current value before running the closure

questions.prompt: What is a `DispatchSemaphore` most fundamentally used for?
questions.explanation: A semaphore maintains a counter that wait() decrements and signal() increments; when the count would go negative, wait() blocks — it's a low-level tool for limiting or serializing access to a resource, independent of Swift's actor model.

options.text: Limiting or serializing access to a resource through a blocking counter
Declaring a closure's captured values as officially safe to send across actor boundaries
Marking a function as eligible to suspend at await points
Automatically retrying a failed asynchronous network request

questions.prompt: A class protected by an internal `NSLock` and an `actor` can both serialize access to mutable state. What's a genuine trade-off between them, not just a style preference?
questions.explanation: A lock-protected class blocks the calling thread while waiting and gives the compiler no way to catch a forgotten lock() call — it's enforced only by convention. An actor's await never blocks a thread, and the compiler rejects unsynchronized access to actor-isolated state at compile time.

options.text: Actors can never be called from synchronous code, while locked classes can be used anywhere
NSLock-based classes are inherently faster, since they avoid Swift's runtime scheduler entirely
Actors require every property to be a value type, unlike locked classes
A lock blocks the thread and isn't checked by the compiler; an actor's await never does

questions.prompt: fetchRowsSynchronously() is a heavy synchronous call with no suspension points inside it. What's the practical problem with calling it directly from this @MainActor async method?
questions.explanation: async doesn't move a function's body off the main thread by itself — this method is @MainActor, so it executes on the main thread, and calling a long synchronous, non-suspending function from it blocks the main thread for its whole duration, exactly as calling it from a non-async method would.

options.text: It won't compile, since @MainActor methods can't call non-async functions
generate automatically runs on a background thread because it's marked async
fetchRowsSynchronously is automatically wrapped in a Task.detached by the compiler
It still runs on the main thread and blocks it, despite generate being async
